title: How Much Does Medical Billing Services Cost? Rates & Pricing Guide
summary: Learn what medical billing services cost, including percentage-of-collections, per-claim and flat-fee pricing, hidden costs, and factors that affect rates.
body_markdown:
As a market reference, several industry pricing guides report percentage-based medical billing fees of about 4% to 10% of net collections. Actual rates vary by specialty, claim volume, payer mix, service scope, and contract terms. These figures are market references rather than standardized industry rates, so practices should compare quotes using the same scope of work and collection definition.


For practices comparing vendors, the lowest headline rate may not represent the lowest


total


cost of medical billing services


. This guide explains medical billing pricing models, what affects rates, potential hidden charges, and how to compare


outsourced medical billing costs


with the cost of an in-house billing operation.


### Key Takeaways


- Medical billing companies use several pricing models, including percentage-based, per-claim, flat-fee, hourly, and hybrid arrangements.


- Medical billing costs vary by claim volume, specialty, claim complexity, payer mix, service scope, and technology requirements.


- Percentage-based fees should be evaluated using the definition of collections, exclusions, minimum fees, and included services.


- Per-claim pricing can make costs more predictable, but the definition of a bill


able claim matter.


- Software, clearinghouse fees, implementation, credentialing, coding, and other services may be priced separately.


- Comparing


total cost, service scope, technology, reporting, and workflow impact provides


more context than comparing billing rates alone.


## How Much Do


Medical Billing Services Cost?


T


here is no single standard medical billing cost for every practice. A billing company’s rate depends on the scope of work, claim volume, specialty, payer mix, technology requirements, and pricing structure. Additional costs may also apply for services such as coding, clearinghouse processing, software, implementation, or credentialing, depending on the agreement.


[Learn about the pros and cons of in-house billing vs. outsourced medical billing. Click here.](https://www2.carecloud.com/rc/in-house-vs-outsourced-billing-ebook?utm_content=in-house-vs-outsourced-billing-display-blog)


For example, a practice that only needs claims submission may have a different cost structure from one seeking full-service revenue cycle management (RCM) covering eligibility, medical coding, claims submission, denial management, payment posting, accounts receivable (A/R) follow-up, and patient billing.


## What


Are the Medical Billing Pricing Models?


[Medical billing companies](https://carecloud.com/top-medical-billing-companies/) use


percentage-of-collections, per-claim, flat-fee, hourly, or hybrid pricing models based on the volume and type of work provided.

### 1. Percentage-of-Collections Pricing


:


Percentage-of-collections pricing ties the billing fee to the collections generated under the agreed pricing terms. This model can align the vendor’s compensation with the practice’s collected revenue, but the contract should clearly define what counts toward the percentage.


Practices should ask:


- Is the percentage based on gross or net collections?


- Are patient payments included?


- Are refunds or take-backs excluded?


- Are certain payer payments excluded?


- Is there a minimum monthly fee or a minimum charge?


- Does the percentage apply to all services or only selected RCM activities?


### 2. Percentage-of-Collections Pricing


:


Under per-claim pricing, the practice pays a predetermined amount for each claim processed. This structure can make medical billing charges easier to estimate:


*Estimated billing cost = number of billable claims x fee per claim*


However, practices should determine whether the vendor charges separately for:


- Corrected claims


- Resubmissions


- Secondary claims


- Paper claims


- Denial appeals


- Patient statements


- Additional claim types


Practices should compare the total expected monthly cost, not just the advertised per-claim rate, because vendors may define a billable claim differently or charge separately for related services.


### 3. Flat-Fee Pricing


:


A flat monthly fee provides a recurring cost regardless of the number of claims within an agreed scope.


This can simplify budgeting, particularly when the practice has


relatively predictable


billing activity.


However, contracts may establish claim-volume limits or additional charges when activity exceeds an agreed threshold.


### 4. Hourly Pricing


:


Hourly


pricing


is


charged according to the time spent performing billing activities. It may be used for specific support functions, temporary projects, or variable workloads. Practices should consider the expected hours, hourly rate, services covered, and whether management or administrative time is billed separately.


### 5. Hybrid Pricing:


Hybrid pricing


combines two or more pricing methods. For example, a vendor may charge a recurring fee for software or administrative support plus a separate fee for selected billing services. Practices should confirm how each


component


is calculated and whether the combined structure creates


additional


fees as claim volume or service needs change.


## What Factors


Affect Medical Billing Service Rates?


[Medical billing services](https://carecloud.com/medical-billing-services/) rates


are primarily affected by claim volume, specialty, claim complexity, payer mix, scope of services, technology requirements, and coding needs.


These factors influence how much work a vendor must perform and whether the engagement requires specialized staff,


additional


technology, or


end-to-end


RCM support.


### 1. Claim Volume


Claim volume can affect pricing because higher volumes generally require more claim processing, payment posting, follow-up, and denial management. V


endors may use monthly claim volume to establish per-claim rates, volume tiers, minimum fees, or other pricing terms.


Practices should provide an expected monthly claim volume when requesting quotes, so vendors can calculate pricing using comparable assumptions.


### 2. Specialty and Claim Complexity


Medical billing rates can vary by specialty because complex procedures, coding requirements, documentation standards, prior authorization, and payer rules can increase the work required to process and follow up on claims.


For example, specialty billing may involve more complex procedures, multiple code sets, modifiers, prior authorization requirements, or payer-specific rules, so practices should ask whether a vendor has experience with their specific specialty rather than assuming a generic billing rate applies equally across specialties.


### 3. Payer Mix


Payer mix can affect billing costs because different payers may have different eligibility, claim submission, authorization, reimbursement, and follow-up requirements.


Practices with a more varied or administratively complex payer mix may require additional billing workflows or follow-up.


When comparing quotes, practices should provide vendors with their major payer categories and approximate claim distribution.


### 4. Service Scope


Service scope is one of the most important factors affecting medical billing cost because vendors may provide anything from basic claims processing to complete RCM support.


A broader RCM engagement may include:


- Insurance eligibility


- Charge capture


- Medical coding


- Claims submission


- Claims follow-up


- Denial management


- Payment posting


- A/R follow-up


- Patient billing


- Collections


- Revenue cycle reporting and analytics


A lower billing rate may not represent a lower total cost if coding, denial management, A/R follow-up, patient billing, or reporting are priced separately.


### 5. EHR and Practice Management Integration


[EHR and practice management integration](https://carecloud.com/practice-management-ehr/) can affect medical billing costs through implementation, interfaces, data migration, configuration, and ongoing support requirements.


Practices should confirm:


- Which EHR and practice management systems the vendor supports


- Whether interfaces and integration setup are included in the quoted price


- Whether setup fees apply


- How data is transferred


- What reporting capabilities are available


- How billing information moves between clinical and financial workflows


### 6. Coding and Documentation Requirements


Coding and documentation requirements can affect billing costs when a practice needs specialized coding, coding audits, documentation review, or additional quality assurance.


Depending on the practice, coding may involve CPT, ICD-10-CM, HCPCS, modifiers, medical necessity requirements, or specialty-specific coding rules.


If coding is excluded from a billing proposal, practices should include the cost of maintaining coding internally or outsourcing it separately when calculating total billing costs.


## What


Does a Medical Billing Fee Actually Include?


A medical billing fee may cover basic claims and payment activities or a broader set of


[RCM services](https://carecloud.com/rcm/) , so practices should verify exactly what is included before comparing prices. A lower billing rate may not mean a lower total cost if coding, denial management, A/R follow-up, patient billing, or reporting are priced separately.


A proposal may include some or all of the following:


- Patient demographic entry


- Insurance eligibility verification


- Charge capture


- Medical coding


- Claims submission


- Clearinghouse processing


- Claim status follow-up


- Denial management


- Payment posting


- A/R follow-up


- Patient billing


- Collections


- Reporting and analytics


Practices should also confirm whether each service is included in the base fee, priced separately, or subject to volume or scope limits.


## Medical Billing vs. RCM


Medical billing primarily covers claim submission and payment-related activities, while revenue cycle management (RCM) can encompass a broader financial workflow from eligibility and coding through:


- Claims


- Denials


- Payment posting


- A/R management


- Patient collections.


A broader RCM engagement may therefore include more services, workflows, technology, and staffing than basic medical billing. This distinction is important when comparing RCM pricing with basic billing fees.


## How


Much Does Revenue Cycle Management Cost?


Revenue cycle management (RCM) costs may vary based on the scope of services, claim volume, specialty, payer mix, technology, and pricing model.


A broader RCM engagement may include eligibility, coding, claims, denial management, payment posting, A/R follow-up, patient billing, and reporting, so its cost cannot be compared directly with a basic claims-processing fee.


For practices evaluating


RCM pricing,


the key is to determine which revenue cycle activities are included in the base fee and which are priced separately. Implementation, technology, coding, clearinghouse services, patient billing, and other specialized services may affect the total cost depending on the agreement.


## What


Hidden Costs Should Practices Look For?


Potential additional costs can include implementation, clearinghouse fees, software, credentialing, coding, patient statements, or services outside the agreed scope.


Not every vendor charges these fees separately, so practices should review what is included in the proposal and how each fee is calculated.


Ask about:


### 1. Implementation and Transition


A vendor may charge for onboarding, data migration, workflow configuration, training, or implementation.


### 2. Clearinghouse Fees


Some billing workflows use a clearinghouse to


transmit


claims and receive payer-related transactions. Confirm whether clearinghouse costs are included in the quoted rate.


### 3. Software


A billing company may provide or integrate practice management or billing software. Ask whether software licensing, user fees, interfaces, or other technology costs are separate.


### 4. Credentialing


Provider enrollment and credentialing may be included in a broader RCM engagement or handled as a separate service.


### 5. Medical Coding


If coding is not included,


determine


whether the practice will handle it internally or pay separately for outsourced coding.


### 6. Patient Billing


Patient statements, payment processing


, patient payment collection


, and related workflows may have separate pricing.


### 7. Additional Volume


Some contracts


establish


a defined volume or scope. Exceeding those limits can trigger


additional


fees.


## Is


Outsourced Medical Billing Cheaper Than In-House Billing?


Not necessarily. Outsourcing should be compared with the total cost of operating the internal billing function, not just employee salaries.


An in-house billing team can involve:


- Salaries and benefits


- Recruitment


- Training


- Management


- Software


- Clearinghouse costs


- Hardware


- Compliance activities


- Paid time off and employee coverage


- Quality assurance


- Continuing education


- Staffing for volume fluctuations


Outsourcing replaces some of these direct and indirect expenses with a vendor fee.


However, outsourcing also introduces costs such as vendor fees, implementation, contract management, and potentially software or services outside the base agreement.

For percentage-based pricing, “applicable collections” should reflect the exact collection base defined in the contract, such as whether patient payments, refunds, recoupments, or other payment categories are included or excluded.


Total estimated billing cost = base billing fee + applicable additional costs


## How


Should You Compare Medical Billing Quotes?


Practices should compare medical billing quotes based on total expected cost, service scope, technology, performance reporting, compliance, and contract terms, not just the advertised billing rate.


Use this checklist when reviewing medical billing service pricing:


### 1. Compare the Pricing Structure


Determine


whether the proposal uses


percentage, per-claim, flat-fee, hourly, or hybrid pricing


.


Estimate the expected monthly and annual cost under the proposed model.


### 2. Define the Billing Base


For percentage pricing,


identify


exactly what


“collections”


means, including which payment types are included or excluded. For per-claim pricing, confirm what qualifies as a


billable claim


.


### 3. Review Included Services


Confirm whether the proposal covers


coding, claims submission and follow-up, denial management, payment posting, A/R management, patient billing, and reporting


.


### 4. Identify


Additional Fees


Ask about


implementation, clearinghouse, software, credentialing, patient statements, coding, and out-of-scope services


.


Confirm whether these are included in the base fee or charged separately.


### 5. Evaluate Technology


Determine


whether the proposal uses


percentage, per-claim, flat-fee, hourly, or hybrid pricing


.


Estimate the expected monthly and annual cost under the proposed model.


### 6. Examine Performance Reporting


Ask which metrics the vendor reports and how often. Relevant measures may include:


- Clean claim rate


- Denial rate


- A/R days


- A/R aging


- Collection rate


- Payment turnaround


- Claim status


- Outstanding patient balances


### 7. Review Compliance and Security


Evaluate how the vendor handles


protected health information (PHI)


and supports applicable


HIPAA privacy and security requirements


.


### 8. Check Contract Terms


Review contract duration, termination provisions, transition responsibilities, data ownership and access, and conditions that could change pricing.


When comparing vendors, normalize each quote to the same scope of services and expected volume. A lower headline rate may not represent a lower total cost if important services or technology are priced separately.


## When


Does Outsourcing Medical Billing Become Financially Worthwhile?


There is no universal revenue, claim volume, or provider-count threshold at which


[outsourcing medical billing](https://carecloud.com/outsource-medical-billing-services/) becomes financially worthwhile.


The decision depends on the practice’s current billing costs, staffing requirements, claim volume, denial and A/R workload, technology needs, administrative burden, and the services included in the outsourced model.


A useful evaluation compares in-house billing cost vs. vendor fees:

n-house

#### 2. Vendor Fees


:

- Services outside the base agreement


- Internal vendor-management time


### Outsourcing May be Worth Considering When:


- Billing workload is increasing faster than internal staffing capacity.


- Denials or A/R backlogs require significant staff time.


- The practice needs specialized coding or billing expertise.


- Technology or reporting capabilities are limited internally.


- Recruiting and retaining billing staff has become difficult.


- Administrative work is taking time away from core practice operations.


- The practice is expanding and needs a more scalable billing model.


The goal is not simply to find the lowest medical billing services cost. It is to determine whether the total cost, service scope, operational capacity, and expected financial performance make the outsourced model a better fit for the practice.


## Conclusion


The


cost of medical billing services


depends on more than a percentage or per-claim fee. Claim volume, specialty, payer mix, service scope, technology, coding requirements, and additional fees can all affect the total cost.


For practices evaluating outsourcing, the most useful comparison is total cost for the same scope of work. Reviewing pricing structure, including services, additional fees, technology, reporting, contract terms, and internal operating costs, can help practices compare vendors on a comparable basis.
